newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Kohl says G7 eco-action over Amazon is "pathetic". [CORRECTED 18:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Kohl says G7 eco-action over Amazon is "pathetic". [CORRECTED 18:25 GMT]

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, paying a visit to Brazil, on Wednesday blasted other Group of Seven industrialised countries for their "pathetic" contribution to the protection of the Amazon rainforest.

Speaking to Brazilian industrialists at a "working breakfast" in the capital Brasilia, the German leader said Bonn was the only G7 nation living up to environmental funding promises made after the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.
"The motto seems to be: The others talk, we pay," he said. "Their actions have been rather pathetic. After all, we are talking about protecting the future of a whole generation."

Germany has taken the lead in funding a pilot programme for saving Brazil's endangered Amazon, the world's largest tropical rainforest, sometimes called the "Lungs of the Earth." The programme, which last week won additional financing from the European Union, a contribution largely bankrolled by Germany, aims to promote sustainable forest use, protection of indigenous communities and ecologically-aware development.

Kohl said Bonn had coughed up 60 percent of the $207 million (corrects from "$312 million") put into the Amazon programme so far, while other G7 industrialised nations were largely sitting on their wallets.

Ecologists are again voicing concern after a recent survey showed the rate of deforestation rising, and Amazon rainforest protection is likely to be placed firmly on the agenda of the next Earth Summit in New York in June 1997.

In July, Brasilia announced a ban on further logging of mahogany and virola hardwood after a Ministry of Science and Technology study revealed 5,750 square miles (14,896 square km) of rainforest was felled in 1994 compared with 4,298 square miles (11,130 square km) in 1991.

Soon after, Brazil dropped its long-standing opposition to the International Tropical Timber Agreement, now likely to come into force next year and limit the $100 billion a year international timber trade to sustainably managed forests.
Kohl, travelling with several high-powered German businessmen on a three-nation Latin American tour aimed at boosting trade and investment, said the environment was "an industry of the future."

He said it was not his prerogative to criticise developing countries that sometimes sacrifice ecology for the sake of progress, especially as Europe had all but eradicated its own forests. "It's not our job to force our help on others, but we can offer it," he said.

On Tuesday, Kohl and Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso spoke of friendship and shared ideals. They pledged to make ties between their countries a priority and to seek ways to boost their $7 billion plus in bilateral trade.
Kohl, who visited Argentina before Brazil, was to fly to Mexico on Wednesday.
